title: Seven ways in which good curriculums can help learning happen
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton sets out seven features that make a curriculum helpful to learning. A good curriculum states clear outcomes framed as knowledge to acquire, abilities to develop or understandings to deepen, because that wording already signals how to teach and assess. It sets stages and ages without dictating week-by-week detail, supports coherent pathways across teachers, offers tried activities that give repeated experiences, and says what matters to assess, with rubrics for skills. He adds that curricula can shift students from doing activities to getting better, citing paired teacher and student versions of outcomes. Finally, curricula should tell parents what and why, making home-school partnership real. A checklist at the end lets readers judge their own curriculum.
points: Clear outcomes opened with knowledge, ability or understanding wording allow teachers to know up front the likely time scale, teaching role and assessment method.
Curriculum should start from learning outcomes, not from activities, teaching instructions or assessment.
Most students, when asked, describe what they are doing rather than what they are learning, so student-friendly versions of the outcomes can shift their attention to improvement.
Curricula should avoid prescribing very short time scales, leaving those to classroom teachers, while still supplying skills rubrics and guidance on what is worth assessing.
Telling parents what learning is intended and why turns home-school partnership into something practical.
quotes: There is so much hanging on the explicit clarity about the learning outcomes. With clarity, we can design activities, orient teaching approaches, choose the best assessment or evaluation techniques, judge how long learning might take and appropriate resources across the school. Without clarity in our learning outcomes, all of this gets fuzzy very quickly.

A well-written curriculum can help that collaboration happen by indicating clearly the sequence and timing of different kinds of learning. A good curriculum makes it easier for teachers to play their part in organising this pathway and, with a little goodwill, easier to trust their colleagues and know what their colleagues are doing.

Remember the difference between students who are busy and those who are busy learning? That difference can happen when activities keep students occupied but are simply not up to the job of helping students get better.

It’s an interesting reflection on the focus of many classrooms that unless we ask a more focused question, almost all children and students tell us what they are doing and not what they are learning. Their thoughts are all about their activity; activity is the focus of their thinking.

What our classroom visits have told us is that there is a gap between what even good teachers think is going on and what children and students think is going on. Teachers might think their lesson is helping students to get better. Most children and students think that their teacher is giving them things to do.

Written well, curriculums can help children and students change their mindset from doing activities to getting better at something. Good curriculums help learning by helping students develop their own focus on and thinking about learning.

The starting point of a curriculum is not the activities that children and students will experience. Those activities should be driven by their appropriateness to the learning outcomes we want our children and students to achieve.
